prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Red Cross President and CEO Mark W. Everson has stepped down after revelations he was "engaged in a personal relationship with a subordinate employee," the organization announced Tuesday. Mark W. Everson says he is leaving his post, effective immediately, for "personal and family reasons." The Red Cross Board of Governors asked for and received Everson's  resignation after it "concluded that the situation reflected poor judgment on Mr. Everson's part and diminished his ability to lead the organization in the future,"  the Red Cross said in a statement on its Web site. Everson, 53, said in a written statement that he was leaving the $500,000-per-year job "for personal and family reasons, and deeply regret it is impossible for me to continue in a job so recently undertaken." Everson -- who is married and has two children -- joined the Red Cross as president and CEO last May. The organization became aware of Everson's relationship with a female Red Cross employee 10 days ago, Chief Public Affairs Officer Suzy C. DeFrancis told CNN in a telephone interview. "I think the board acted very quickly," she said, adding that the woman remains in her job. About Everson, DeFrancis said, "We're grateful for his service." The board of governors on Tuesday appointed Mary S. Elcano, general counsel and five-year Red Cross employee, as interim president and CEO. Everson had worked in the Bush administration from August 2001 -- including serving as commissioner of the Internal Revenue Service -- until he was hired by the Red Cross. "This is flabbergasting, that's all I can say. It's completely contrary to his public persona that he evidenced while he was at the IRS," said Suzanne Ross McDowell, a Washington-based attorney who served on an advisory committee to the IRS division that deals with tax-exempt organizations. "From the standpoint of exempt organizations on the non-profit sector, it's just another news story that we would rather not see," she said. "It's got nothing to do with the Red Cross," said Ira Milstein, a New York lawyer specializing in corporate governance who has worked with the organization and was impressed with Everson. "He was a team player and a good leader. To have him fall off a cliff like this is just sad." A search committee has been formed to begin the process of finding Everson's permanent replacement, the organization said. The job has been a challenging one. Marsha J. Evans resigned as president in 2005, after the Red Cross response to Hurricane Katrina came under fire. Four years earlier, Bernadine Healy quit the post after the organization was criticized for mishandling donations intended for victims of the September 11 terrorist attacks and collecting vast quantities of blood that was not needed and ultimately thrown out. Healy told reporters she "had no choice" about her resignation. Meanwhile, DeFrancis acknowledged Tuesday that, 14 years after a court ordered the agency to improve its collection of blood, it has yet to meet federal safety and quality-control requirements. (CNN) — The American Red Cross announced Tuesday that President and CEO Mark W. Everson had resigned after the organization learned he had been involved in a personal relationship with an employee who reported to him.

Everson said his departure was immediate and attributed it to “personal and family reasons.” According to a statement posted on the Red Cross website, its Board of Governors requested and accepted his resignation after determining that his conduct showed poor judgment and undermined his capacity to lead the organization going forward.

In a written statement, Everson, 53, said he was giving up the position, which paid $500,000 annually, because of personal and family considerations. He added that he deeply regretted being unable to remain in a role he had taken on only recently.

Everson, who is married and has two children, became the Red Cross president and chief executive in May. Chief Public Affairs Officer Suzy C. DeFrancis told CNN by telephone that the organization first learned 10 days earlier of his relationship with a female Red Cross employee. DeFrancis said the board responded promptly and confirmed that the woman continues to work for the organization. She also expressed appreciation for Everson’s service.

On Tuesday, the Board of Governors selected Mary S. Elcano to serve as interim president and CEO. Elcano is the organization’s general counsel and has worked for the Red Cross for five years.

Before joining the Red Cross, Everson served in the Bush administration beginning in August 2001. His government roles included commissioner of the Internal Revenue Service, where he remained until the Red Cross hired him.

Washington attorney Suzanne Ross McDowell, who served on an advisory committee connected to the IRS division responsible for tax-exempt organizations, said the news was astonishing and entirely inconsistent with the public image Everson had presented while leading the IRS. She added that those working with nonprofit and tax-exempt organizations would prefer not to see another negative story involving the sector.

Ira Milstein, a New York corporate-governance attorney who has worked with the Red Cross and had been impressed by Everson, said the matter did not reflect on the organization itself. He described Everson as cooperative and an effective leader, calling his abrupt downfall sad.

The Red Cross said it had established a search committee to begin looking for a permanent successor.

Leadership of the organization has proved difficult in recent years. Marsha J. Evans left the presidency in 2005 after the Red Cross was criticized over its response to Hurricane Katrina. Four years before that, Bernadine Healy resigned following criticism that the organization had mishandled money donated for victims of the September 11 terrorist attacks. The Red Cross was also faulted for collecting far more blood than was needed, with the excess ultimately being discarded. Healy told reporters at the time that she had “no choice” but to step down.

Separately, DeFrancis acknowledged Tuesday that the Red Cross still had not satisfied federal safety and quality-control standards for blood collection, despite a court order issued 14 years earlier requiring the organization to improve its practices.

counterfactuals.output:
Mark W. Everson resigned in November 2007 after only about six months as president and chief executive of the American Red Cross. He acknowledged having a personal, reportedly consensual, relationship with a female subordinate. After an internal review, the board concluded that the relationship reflected poor judgment and undermined his ability to lead. It requested and immediately accepted his resignation; the employee involved also left the organization. Board chair Bonnie McElveen-Hunter expressed “deep disappointment” while emphasizing that the Red Cross had acted promptly and according to its ethics policies.

Everson had come to the Red Cross after serving as IRS commissioner from 2003 to 2007. At the IRS, he had developed a reputation as a tough, disciplined administrator who strengthened tax-law enforcement, pursued abusive tax shelters and scrutinized nonprofit organizations’ political activity. That record made the disclosure especially surprising to former colleagues and tax-policy observers, who had generally regarded him as highly ethical and serious about institutional integrity.

Nonprofit-governance experts largely said the board had little choice but to act because a relationship between a chief executive and a subordinate creates conflicts of interest and exposes an organization to legal and reputational risk. Some praised the board’s decisiveness, but others said the episode deepened concerns about whether the Red Cross’s governance structure and board-management relationship made the top job unusually difficult.

The resignation added to years of instability at the organization. Bernadine Healy had departed in 2001 after clashes with the board, including disputes over the handling of post-September 11 donations. Marsha Evans was forced out in 2005 following tensions with directors, and the organization then operated under interim leadership before hiring Everson. His abrupt exit—amid broader governance reforms and criticism of the Red Cross’s responses to major disasters—left the charity searching yet again for stable leadership.

# American Red Cross Names Mary S. Elcano Interim President After Everson Resigns

**WASHINGTON, Nov. 27, 2007** — The American Red Cross has appointed longtime senior executive Mary S. Elcano as interim president and chief executive following the resignation of Mark W. Everson, whose brief tenure ended after the organization learned that he had engaged in a personal relationship with a subordinate employee.

Elcano, the charity’s general counsel and corporate secretary, will oversee the Red Cross while its governing board conducts a search for a permanent leader. Her appointment places an experienced internal official at the head of one of the nation’s largest humanitarian organizations at a time of renewed leadership upheaval.

In announcing Everson’s departure, the Red Cross said its board acted after becoming aware of the relationship.

“The Board acted quickly after learning that Mr. Everson had engaged in a personal relationship with a subordinate employee,” the organization said in a statement. “It concluded that the situation reflected poor judgment on Mr. Everson’s part and diminished his ability to lead the organization in the future.”

The Red Cross said the matter was not connected to its programs, disaster-relief work or finances. Even so, Everson’s resignation represents another disruption for an institution that has spent years trying to restore public confidence following criticism of its disaster response, fundraising practices and internal governance.

Everson, a former commissioner of the Internal Revenue Service, had taken over the Red Cross only in May. At the time, the organization presented him as a reform-minded executive whose government and management experience could help stabilize the charity.

In a statement accompanying his resignation, Everson said, “I am resigning for personal and family reasons, and deeply regret it is impossible for me to continue a job so recently undertaken.”

## Elcano brings institutional experience

Elcano joined the Red Cross in the early 1980s and rose to become its top legal officer. As general counsel and corporate secretary, she worked closely with the board and senior management on governance, regulatory and organizational matters. Her selection as interim president offers continuity while the charity again searches for a permanent chief executive.

Her immediate responsibilities will include maintaining the Red Cross’s nationwide disaster-response network, supporting local chapters, overseeing blood-collection operations and reassuring employees, volunteers and donors that the latest leadership change will not interrupt services.

The board did not immediately announce a timetable for choosing Everson’s successor.

Elcano inherits an organization with a distinctive public role. Although the American Red Cross is not a federal agency, it operates under a congressional charter and frequently works alongside federal, state and local authorities during major disasters. It also manages a large share of the nation’s blood supply and provides emergency communications and other assistance to military families.

That visibility has made its management problems particularly damaging. Decisions by Red Cross leaders are often scrutinized not only by donors but also by Congress, regulators and communities that depend on the organization after hurricanes, floods, fires and other emergencies.

## A succession of leadership disputes

Everson’s departure follows several years of controversy at the top of the organization.

In 2001, President Bernadine Healy resigned amid disputes with the board over management and over the handling of money raised after the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. The Red Cross had created the Liberty Fund to receive post-attack donations, but it faced intense criticism after indicating that some of the money might be reserved for future terrorism preparedness rather than distributed entirely to people affected by the attacks.

Under public and congressional pressure, the organization changed course and pledged to devote the fund to Sept. 11-related needs. The episode damaged donor trust and intensified questions about how clearly the Red Cross explained the intended use of restricted contributions.

Healy was succeeded by Marsha J. Evans, a retired Navy rear admiral who became president in 2002. Evans sought to modernize the charity and improve coordination among its national headquarters and hundreds of local chapters. But she stepped down in December 2005 after losing the board’s support.

Her departure came as the Red Cross was facing severe criticism over its response to Hurricane Katrina. The charity mounted one of the largest relief efforts in its history, sheltering and feeding large numbers of evacuees, but it was also faulted for uneven coordination, difficulty reaching some of the hardest-hit communities, and weaknesses in financial controls.

The Katrina response generated complaints about waste, fraud and the organization’s ability to track assistance. Red Cross officials said the unprecedented scale of the disaster placed extraordinary demands on its systems, but the criticism added urgency to calls for structural reform.

Following Evans’s exit, Jack McGuire served as interim president and chief executive. Everson was then chosen as the permanent leader, raising hopes that the organization had ended a period of instability.

His resignation after roughly six months means the Red Cross must begin another search while continuing reforms already under way.

## Governance reforms under scrutiny

Congress and the organization’s own review panels have pushed the Red Cross to clarify the roles of its board and management, improve oversight and modernize a governance structure widely viewed as cumbersome.

The charity’s congressional charter was revised in 2007, reducing the size of its board and seeking to make directors more accountable. The changes were intended to address concerns that the previous board was too large to provide effective oversight and that responsibility was too dispersed among national leaders and semi-autonomous local chapters.

Everson’s departure is likely to test those reforms. The board’s rapid action suggests a desire to demonstrate stronger oversight and avoid a prolonged scandal. At the same time, the loss of another chief executive may revive concerns that frequent turnover is making it difficult to carry out long-term changes.

Bonnie McElveen-Hunter, chairman of the Red Cross board, emphasized in the organization’s announcement that its humanitarian work would continue despite the transition. The decision to turn to Elcano, a veteran of the institution who understands both its legal obligations and internal structure, appears designed to minimize disruption.

For Elcano, the challenge will be both operational and symbolic. She must keep the organization focused on disaster relief, blood services and military-family assistance while helping the board navigate another sensitive leadership search.

The Red Cross remains one of the country’s best-known charities, sustained by millions of donors and volunteers. But Everson’s abrupt exit underscores a persistent problem: an organization built to respond quickly to other people’s crises is once again confronting a crisis of leadership of its own.
